Title: Imaging Mexico "Imaging Mexico” (CRN 49964) explores how since the post-independence period in the early 1800s through the present, visual cultures have participated in and commented on the formation of national identity in Mexico. We will study a variety of textual and visual mediums including the novel, painting, sculpture, architecture, prints, crafts, photography, and film in order to analyze how these various cultural forms have contributed to a variety of national projects. Students will hone the capacity to speak and write analytically about various forms of cultural production using each medium’s corresponding terminology in Spanish. Students will also acquire knowledge of major historical, artistic, and intellectual figures of the modern period in Mexico and a familiarity with critical approaches to cultural studies. Class meetings will take place on Tues. and Thurs. from 11:00 am - 12:20 pm. Language of instruction is Spanish. This course fulfills 300-level course requirements for the Spanish major or minor. Enrollment requires completion of SPAN 228 or permission by instructor. If the course is full, students can add their names to the waitlist at go.illinois.edu/SPAN_waitlist

Language & Minorities in Europe. Credit: 3 or 4 hours. Survey of regional and immigrant minority language use, policies, and planning across Europe. Focus on political and social issues, such as language regimes, education, loss, and maintenance. Two immigrant languages, Turkish and Arabic/Berber, and four indigenous language families: Balto-Slavic with Estonian, Celtic, Romance with Basque, and Slavic with Hungarian. Taught in English. Same as GER 418, ITAL 418, LING 418, PS 418, SLAV 418, SPAN 418, and EURO 418. 3 undergraduate hours. 4 graduate hours.

Topic Title: Bodies In this course, we will explore how various sorts of embodiment shaped and reflected cultural values and norms of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries in Spain. We'll discuss works that revolve around the significance of phenotype, of sex, and of "blood," among other notions; that instruct Spaniards about how to control the vagaries of our bodies; and that, every now and then, remind readers that bodies might be a source of pleasure. We'll study big novels, poetry, and drama, but also newspapers of the period, manuals, and other bodies of work. Prerequisites: SPAN 312 and SPAN 320.

Topic Title: Archival Futures, Colonial Pasts: Rethinking the Latin American Archive Early definitions of the Spanish word “archivo” describe the archive as a “public space”—a place where “original” documents and artifacts are preserved. It underscores the importance of preserving for posterity as a way to protect cultural heritage. These early definitions also emphasize the significance of treating what is preserved as something of utmost value. In the 18th century, it was also conceived as something that needed to be kept but “in perfect order” so that it is not lost or damaged. The act of care and vigilance with which something is kept was equally important. However, for contemporary critics such as Ann Laura Stoler, archives are not merely spaces that store documents, but they are also spaces that record the movements and emotions of the people mentioned in the documents. She adds, “they are records of uncertainty and doubt on how people imagined they could and might make the rubrics of rule correspond to a changing imperial world” (4). For this reason, we should read archival documents “against the grain” which means reflecting, paying attention to sound, emotions, and what is at first glance unintelligible. This course moves beyond conventional understandings of the colonial archive as a repository of knowledge to examine how the voices of marginalized groups—including women, Black, and Indigenous peoples—have been both preserved and silenced through archival practices. Through engagement with key theoretical readings, we will explore what constitutes an archive, how archival formations shape historical narratives, and how the concept of the archive has evolved over time. Particular attention will be given to the ways archives can serve as sites of both exclusion and resistance, while opening new possibilities for recovering and interpreting marginalized histories. Furthermore, we will examine current archival approaches in which different types of non-written materials are considered as materials to be preserved. How do we record visual images, sounds, oral traditions, movements, bodies, material objects, race, sexuality, emotions and identities in general, will constitute key points of discussion. In addition to hosting classes in the Rare Book and Manuscript Library at UIUC, this class will include guest lectures from UIUC librarians, and also experts on archival studies from outside the university. Primary texts to be analyzed include chronicles, natural histories, colonial newspapers, museum exhibitions, visual representations such as maps, graffiti and paintings, legal cases, digital catalogs, and literary anthologies. Class will be conducted in Spanish.
